entities.summary:
Basilides, active in Alexandria during the early 2nd century CE, emerged as one of the most intellectually sophisticated and influential Gnostic teachers, challenging the nascent proto-orthodox Christian movement with a complex theological system. Born around 117 CE and dying near 140 CE, Basilides founded a distinct school that attracted numerous adherents, particularly in Egypt, during a period of intense philosophical and religious syncretism. His teachings were not merely a deviation but a profound reinterpretation of Christian narratives through a Hellenistic philosophical lens, making him a central figure in the theological debates that shaped the contours of early Christianity.

At the core of Basilides' doctrine was a radically transcendent, unknowable God, from whom a sequence of spiritual entities, or Aeons, emanated to form the cosmos. He posited a dualistic understanding of reality, where the material world was inferior and distinct from the divine realm, and salvation was achieved through gnosis—secret knowledge—rather than faith or deeds. Basilides taught a form of docetism, asserting that Christ's physical body was an illusion, and thus his suffering on the cross was not real. His extensive exegetical work, particularly his commentaries on the Gospels known as the *Exegetica*, sought to provide a systematic and philosophical foundation for his unique cosmology and soteriology.

His ideas compelled proto-orthodox writers to define Christian beliefs more precisely, shaping the trajectory of Christian theology for centuries.
